To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the number of friends sharing the same consumption patterns is a good indicator for the virality (i.e. the number of friends that will consume a given content) of contents, (2) the number of active users (i.e. influencers) does not affect the popularity of a content, and (3) polarization (i.e. exposure to conspiracy theories) may be the driving force behind the virality of misinformation.

(1) users tend to engage with similar contents (homophily) in the social network, and (2) in an environment where the consumption of conspiracy stories (polarity) is pervasive, users with similar consumption patterns are more likely to engage with the same contents (homophilic polarization) which may lead to the virality of misinformation.
